items.prompt:
Which mark goes at the end of this sentence?
Where did you put my shoes___

options.text: a full stop
options.why: A full stop ends a statement. This sentence asks something.

options.text: an exclamation mark
options.why: An exclamation mark shows strong feeling. This sentence asks something.

options.text: a question mark
a comma
options.why: A comma does not end a sentence.

hints: Is the sentence telling, asking or shouting?
Questions need a special mark at the end.
Look at the first word: Where.
items.explanation: The sentence asks a question, so it ends with a question mark.

items.prompt: Sort the sentences by the mark they need at the end.
hints: Decide if each sentence tells, asks or shows strong feeling.
Sentences that begin with Where or Can are usually questions.
Start with What a huge wave. Is it a calm fact or a loud feeling?
items.explanation: Statements end with a full stop, questions end with a question mark and sentences showing strong feeling can end with an exclamation mark.

items.prompt: Put the words in order. End with the right mark.
hints: The sentence shows strong feeling.
It starts with What a.
The word with the mark at the end goes last.
items.explanation: The sentence shows surprise, so it ends with an exclamation mark.

options.text: “Where is my hat?” asked Dad.
“Where is my hat,” asked Dad.
options.why: This is a question, so it needs a question mark instead of a comma.

options.text: “Where is my hat”? asked Dad.
options.why: The question mark belongs inside the speech marks.

options.text: “Where is my hat?”. asked Dad.
options.why: There should not be a full stop after the speech marks here.

hints: Dad is asking a question.
The mark that shows a question belongs with the spoken words.
Check where the question mark is: inside or outside the speech marks?
items.explanation: The question mark is part of the words Dad says, so it goes inside the closing speech marks. Asked Dad is not a new sentence.

items.prompt: Sekar says something. Then Kofi replies. What should the writer do when Kofi starts to speak?

options.text: write Kofi's words on the same line without speech marks
options.why: Each speaker needs speech marks around their own words.

options.text: use capital letters for all of Kofi's words
options.why: Kofi's words do not all need capital letters.

options.text: put a comma before Kofi's words
options.why: A comma does not show a new speaker.

options.text: start a new line for Kofi's words

hints: Think about how a play or a story shows who is talking.
A new speaker means a change.
The writer starts a new line each time.
items.explanation: We start a new line for each new speaker. This helps the reader see who is talking.

items.prompt: Put the words in order. Use the comma in the right place.
hints: The spoken words come first.
The comma goes before the closing speech mark.
Kofi is the last word.
items.explanation: The spoken words are first, with a comma inside the closing speech marks. Then the reporting clause said Kofi finishes the sentence.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to make a correct sentence.
hints: The sentence begins with the speaker.
A comma goes after said.
The spoken words end with a full stop inside the speech marks.
items.explanation: When we name the speaker first, we put a comma after said. The spoken words follow in speech marks and end with a full stop inside.

items.prompt: Put the parts in order to make split speech.
hints: Split speech has a speaker in the middle.
There is a comma after each part before the speech marks.
Which part opens the sentence with a speech mark?
items.explanation: The sentence reads: “Please,” said Ines, “close the window.” Her words are split by the words said Ines.

items.prompt: Choose all the sentences that are punctuated correctly.

options.text: “I like your drawing,” said Wulan.
Bayu asked, “Can I borrow your ruler?”
“Time to go” said Mum.
options.why: A comma is missing before the closing speech marks.

options.text: “Where are we going?”, asked Leo.
options.why: A comma should not follow a question mark.

options.text: Yuki shouted, “Catch the ball!”
“Well done.” said Dad.
options.why: Inside the speech marks, a comma replaces the full stop when the speaker follows.

hints: Check each sentence one by one.
When the speaker comes after the speech, a comma, ? or ! goes inside the closing marks.
A question mark and a comma should not sit side by side.
items.explanation: The correct sentences use a comma, question mark or exclamation mark inside the speech marks. The others have a missing comma or a mark in the wrong place.

options.text: “I am tired,” said Leo “but I will finish.”
options.why: A comma is missing after said Leo.

options.text: “I am tired,” said Leo, “but I will finish.”
“I am tired” said Leo, “but I will finish.”
options.why: A comma is missing inside the first closing speech mark.

options.text: “I am tired,” said Leo. “but I will finish.”
options.why: A full stop would start a new sentence, but but carries on the first one.

hints: The speaker interrupts one sentence.
After said Leo, the sentence carries on.
Check for a comma after the first piece of speech and after the speaker.
items.explanation: The speech is one sentence that is split in two. The second part carries on, so it begins with a small letter: but.

items.prompt:
Choose the right mark for each gap.
Mum said___ “Yes, after your homework___”
hints: The first gap comes after the speaker, before the speech marks.
A comma joins the speaker to the spoken words.
The spoken words end with a sentence mark inside the speech marks.
items.explanation: A comma comes after said when the speaker comes first. The spoken sentence ends with a full stop inside the speech marks.

items.prompt: Which sentence needs a question mark at the end?

options.text: Ask Mum where the key is
options.why: This is a command, so it needs a full stop.

options.text: Do you know where the key is
I wonder where the key is
options.why: This tells us what someone thinks, so it needs a full stop.

options.text: Tell me where the key is
options.why: This is a command, so it needs a full stop.

hints: Look for a sentence that asks something directly.
Questions often begin with words like do, can, where or why.
Which sentence waits for someone to answer?
items.explanation: Do you know where the key is asks a direct question. The other sentences tell or ask in a different way, so they end with full stops.

items.prompt: Which sentence should end with an exclamation mark?

options.text: The sun rose over the hills
options.why: This is a calm statement.

options.text: I will bake a cake tomorrow
options.why: This is a plain statement.

options.text: The cake is on the table
options.why: This is a plain statement.

options.text: What a gigantic cake

hints: An exclamation mark shows strong feeling.
Which sentence shows surprise or wonder?
Read each one with a loud, surprised voice.
items.explanation: What a gigantic cake shows surprise, so it can end with an exclamation mark. The others simply tell us facts.

items.prompt:
Which is the best way to write this with correct punctuation?
mum asked can you pass the salt

options.text: Mum asked, “Can you pass the salt?”
Mum asked “can you pass the salt.”
options.why: The spoken words need a capital letter and a question mark.

options.text: Mum asked, “Can you pass the salt.”
options.why: This asks a question, so it needs a question mark.

options.text: Mum asked, “Can you pass the salt”?
options.why: The question mark belongs inside the speech marks.

hints: Look for names, spoken words and a question.
Spoken words start with a capital letter.
Decide which end mark the spoken words need.
items.explanation: A comma follows asked. The question starts with a capital and ends with a question mark inside the speech marks.

items.prompt: Which sentence asks Grandma to join in the eating?

options.text: Let’s eat Grandma.
options.why: Without a comma this sounds as if Grandma is the meal.

options.text: Let’s, eat Grandma.
options.why: The comma is in the wrong place.

options.text: Let’s eat, Grandma.
Lets eat Grandma.
options.why: Lets has no apostrophe, and the sentence still has no comma.

hints: Commas can change the meaning of a sentence.
Who is being spoken to?
A comma goes before the name of the person we are talking to.
items.explanation: A comma before Grandma shows that we are speaking to her. Without the comma, the sentence says we are going to eat her!

options.text: I packed a towel a hat, sunscreen and a book.
options.why: A comma is missing after towel.

options.text: I packed, a towel, a hat, sunscreen and a book.
options.why: There should not be a comma after packed.

options.text: I packed a towel, a hat, sunscreen and a book.
I packed a towel, a hat, sunscreen, and, a book.
options.why: Too many commas break up the list.

hints: In a list, commas separate the items.
The last two items are joined with and.
Check that the comma is not after packed.
items.explanation: We use commas to separate the things in a list. The last two items are joined by and, so there is no comma before it here.

items.prompt: Sort the sentences. Are they punctuated correctly?
hints: Look at the mark just before the closing speech marks.
If the speaker comes before the speech, a comma follows said or asked.
If the speaker comes after the speech, the mark goes inside the closing marks.
items.explanation: The correct sentences use a comma, question mark or exclamation mark inside the closing speech marks, or a comma after said. The others miss a mark or use the wrong one.
